questions.q: Price rises from $10 to $12 and quantity demanded falls from 1,000 to 900. Calculate PED (ignore the sign, give one decimal).
questions.fb: Use percentage changes on the original value: %ΔP = 2 ÷ 10 = 20%, %ΔQ = 100 ÷ 1,000 = 10%. PED = 10 ÷ 20 = 0.5. Revisit the PED formula in the Learn tab.

questions.q: Incomes rise by 5% and demand for a good rises by 15%. Calculate YED.
questions.fb: YED = %ΔQd ÷ %ΔY = 15 ÷ 5 = 3. A figure above 1 suggests a luxury or income-elastic good.

questions.q: The price of good B rises by 10% and demand for good A falls by 25%. Calculate XED, including the sign.
questions.hint: Include the minus sign if it is negative.
questions.fb: XED = %ΔQd of A ÷ %ΔP of B = −25 ÷ 10 = −2.5. Keep the sign for XED, because it shows whether the goods are substitutes or complements.

questions.q: A good has a PED of 0.4. If its price rises, what is likely to happen to total revenue?
questions.ok: Correct: demand is inelastic, so quantity falls proportionally less than price rises.
questions.fb: With PED below 1 (inelastic), the % fall in quantity is smaller than the % rise in price, so revenue tends to rise. See the revenue table in the Learn tab.

questions.q: A firm cuts the price of a product with PED = 1.8. What is likely to happen to its revenue?
questions.ok: Correct: elastic demand means a price cut tends to raise revenue.
questions.fb: PED above 1 (elastic): the % rise in quantity is bigger than the % fall in price, so revenue tends to rise. See Lab 1 in the Explore tab.

questions.q: A negative YED indicates which type of good?
questions.fb: A negative income elasticity means demand falls as income rises, which is the definition of an inferior good. Examples include own-brand value ranges.

questions.ok: Full marks: responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in price.
questions.fb: Two parts: it measures the responsiveness (how much) of quantity demanded, to a change in the good's own price. Revisit 'Three elasticities of demand' in the Learn tab.
questions.model: PED measures the responsiveness of quantity demanded of a product to a change in its own price, ceteris paribus.
questions.fb_part: Part marks: some of your answer earned credit, but not all. Two parts: it measures the responsiveness (how much) of quantity demanded, to a change in the good's own price. Revisit 'Three elasticities of demand' in the Learn tab.

questions.q: State three factors that could affect the price elasticity of demand for a product.
questions.fb: Three different determinants are needed, such as availability of substitutes, relative expense, time period, necessity or luxury, addiction and brand loyalty. See 'What determines PED?' in the Learn tab.
questions.model: Availability and closeness of substitutes (more substitutes tends to make demand more elastic); the proportion of income spent on it (larger share, more elastic); and the time period (longer run, more elastic).
questions.fb_part: Part marks: some of your answer earned credit, but not all. Three different determinants are needed, such as availability of substitutes, relative expense, time period, necessity or luxury, addiction and brand loyalty. See 'What determines PED?' in the Learn tab.

questions.q: The XED between butter and margarine is +1.8. What type of relationship does this show?
questions.ok: Correct: a positive XED suggests substitutes.
questions.fb: A positive XED means that when the price of one good rises, demand for the other rises too, which is how substitutes behave. Negative would suggest complements.

questions.q: Along a straight-line demand curve, where is demand most price elastic?
opts: At a high price, low quantity
At a low price, high quantity
questions.ok: Correct: at high prices, small absolute changes are large percentage changes.
questions.fb: The slope is constant but PED is not, because it uses percentages. At the top left a small change in quantity is a large percentage change, so demand is more elastic. Watch the animation in the Watch tab.
questions.model: At a high price, low quantity
